gloss_terse: Jaare-Oregim, father of Elhanan mentioned in 2 Samuel 21:19; likely a scribal error
gloss_readable: This proper name appears in 2 Samuel 21:19 as the father of Elhanan, one of David's warriors. Most scholars view it as a textual corruption, comparing it with the parallel account in 1 Chronicles 20:5 which reads "Jair." The name may have arisen from scribal anticipation of "Oregim" (weavers) in the following line, leading to a compound form that doesn't appear elsewhere in Scripture.

senses.1: Appears only in 2 Samuel 21:19 in connection with Elhanan's genealogy. The widespread scholarly consensus, reflected in BDB and textual commentaries, is that this represents a corrupted reading. The multilingual glosses preserve the unusual form (Oregim, Yaare) while recognizing its problematic status through question marks and brackets in some traditions.

gloss_terse: Yaasu/Yaasai, an Israelite who married a foreign wife during Ezra's reforms (Ezra 10:37)
gloss_readable: This name appears twice in Ezra 10:37, once in the consonantal text (Ketiv) and once in the marginal reading (Qere), representing a common scribal practice of preserving variant readings. The individual is listed among those who had taken foreign wives and were compelled to divorce them during Ezra's religious reforms. The Septuagint renders it as "and they did," suggesting some textual confusion in the Greek tradition.

senses.1: Found exclusively in Ezra 10:37 among the list of men with foreign wives. The dual attestation (Ketiv/Qere) shows textual uncertainty about the precise vocalization. Spanish and English preserve both forms (Yaasu/Yaasai), while French and German maintain the Hebrew consonantal spelling in brackets, reflecting the manuscript variation.

gloss_terse: Yaasiel, the name of two men: a warrior of David (1 Chr 11:47) and a Benjamite ruler (1 Chr 27:21)
gloss_readable: This personal name designates two distinct individuals in the Chronicler's genealogies and military rosters. The first Yaasiel was one of David's mighty warriors listed in the expanded roster found only in Chronicles. The second served as a tribal leader over Benjamin during David's administrative organization. The name appears with the conjunction "and" in one occurrence, showing its integration into narrative lists.

senses.1: Attested in 1 Chronicles 11:47 and 27:21 for two separate individuals. The Septuagint variations (Iessiēl, Aseiēr, Iassiēl) show the expected Greek adaptation of the Hebrew name. Multilingual glosses preserve both the simple form and the conjunctive form, with French and German maintaining Hebrew script in brackets to indicate textual precision.

gloss_terse: A reduplicative adjective meaning "very pretty" or "beautiful," used of Egypt as a heifer in Jeremiah 46:20
gloss_readable: This unusual form appears only in Jeremiah 46:20, where Egypt is compared to a beautiful heifer. The word employs reduplication, a Hebrew device that intensifies meaning or adds a diminutive quality, similar to forms like "reddish" or "greenish." BDB suggests the original vocalization was likely "yephephiyyah" rather than the Masoretic "yepheh-piyyah." The Septuagint translates it as "adorned" or "beautified," capturing the aesthetic dimension.

senses.1: Exclusively used in Jeremiah 46:20 in the prophetic oracle against Egypt. The reduplicative structure creates emphasis on the heifer's beauty, making the coming judgment more striking. Spanish renders it straightforwardly as "hermosa" (beautiful), while French and German preserve the Hebrew components in brackets, acknowledging the compound's unusual morphology.

gloss_terse: Brightness, splendor; used of the glory of the prince of Tyre in Ezekiel 28:7, 17
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes radiant beauty or splendor, appearing only in Ezekiel's oracle against the prince of Tyre. The prophet uses it twice with a pronominal suffix ("your splendor") to describe the magnificent glory that will be profaned and destroyed. The word captures both physical brilliance and the honor or majesty associated with royal power, making its destruction all the more dramatic in the prophetic judgment scene.

senses.1: Found exclusively in Ezekiel 28:7 and 17 within the taunt against Tyre's ruler. The context emphasizes hubris and coming humiliation: the splendor that led to pride will be cast down. Spanish "esplendor" and French "briller" both capture the luminous quality, while German preserves the Hebrew form, reflecting the word's rare and specialized usage.

gloss_terse: Iphtah-el, a valley forming a boundary between Zebulun and Asher (Joshua 19:14, 27)
gloss_readable: This place name means "God opens" and designates a valley that served as a tribal boundary marker in the Promised Land allotments. Located near Jefat (ancient Jotapata), it likely corresponds to the upper portion of Wady Abellin in Galilee. The valley appears in Joshua's boundary descriptions for both Zebulun and Asher, marking a shared geographic reference point between the two northern tribes.

senses.1: Attested in Joshua 19:14 and 27 in boundary contexts. The Septuagint shows variation (Gaiphael, Gai kai Phthaiel) in attempting to render the compound Hebrew name. All major translation traditions preserve the proper-name status, with slight variations in transliteration (Jifta-el in Spanish, Yiphtach-El in English and others).

gloss_terse: Adjective meaning "going forth," used with a pronominal suffix to mean "those who came from his loins"
gloss_readable: This participial adjective appears only in 2 Chronicles 32:21, where it describes "those who came forth from [Sennacherib's] loins," a euphemism for his own sons. The text exhibits the common Ketiv/Qere variation, with the consonantal text using a singular suffix and the marginal reading preferring a plural. The parallel passage in Isaiah 37:38 simply uses "his sons," making the Chronicles reading more circumlocutory.

senses.1: Found in 2 Chronicles 32:21 describing the assassins of the Assyrian king Sennacherib. The phrase "those going forth from his loins" employs a biological metaphor for offspring. Multilingual traditions vary: Spanish and English offer expanded glosses ("those who went out from his loins"), while French and German preserve the Hebrew in brackets, acknowledging the unusual euphemistic construction.

gloss_terse: A casting (of metal); technical term for the molten bronze casting process used in temple construction
gloss_readable: This feminine noun appears in the description of Solomon's temple furnishings, specifically the ornamental gourds cast in bronze. The phrase "cast in its casting" emphasizes the method of manufacture through molten metal poured into molds. The parallel passage in 2 Chronicles 4:3 uses a different vocalization (mutsaqtô), showing textual variation in how scribes understood this specialized metallurgical vocabulary.

senses.1: Attested in 1 Kings 7:24 and 30 in temple construction contexts. The term highlights the technical artistry of Hiram's bronze work, where decorative elements were formed through molten metal casting rather than carving or welding. Spanish "fundición" and French "jeta" both capture the casting process, while German preserves the verbal root, reflecting the technical nature of ancient Near Eastern metallurgy.

gloss_terse: Obedience; used with both subjective genitive (obedience of peoples) and objective genitive (obedience to mother)
gloss_readable: This rare feminine noun denotes the act or quality of obedience, appearing only twice in poetic contexts. In Genesis 49:10 it appears in Jacob's blessing of Judah, referring to "the obedience of the peoples" that will come to the Davidic ruler. In Proverbs 30:17, it describes the moral duty of obedience to one's mother. The word's flexibility with genitive constructions shows its capacity to express both who obeys and who is obeyed.

senses.1: Found in Genesis 49:10 (Jacob's oracle) and Proverbs 30:17 (wisdom saying). The Genesis passage carries messianic weight in Jewish and Christian interpretation, referring to a future king to whom nations will submit. Multilingual glosses preserve both the subjective form (obedience of) and objective form (obedience to), reflecting the Hebrew construct chain's directional ambiguity in these contexts.

gloss_terse: Burning; used figuratively for divine judgment in Isaiah 10:16
gloss_readable: This verbal noun derives from the root meaning "to burn" and appears twice in Isaiah 10:16, both as an absolute form and as a construct. The prophet uses it to describe Yahweh's coming judgment against Assyria, depicted as a consuming fire that will kindle beneath the invader's glory. The repetition ("burning... burning") creates intensity, emphasizing the totality and inevitability of divine retribution.

senses.1: Exclusively attested in Isaiah 10:16 in a prophetic oracle against Assyria. The context is thoroughly metaphorical: God will send leanness among Assyria's stout warriors and kindle a burning beneath their glory. French and German preserve the Hebrew forms in brackets, while Spanish "encendimiento" and English "burning" capture the fiery destruction inherent in the root verb.

gloss_terse: Yaqim, the name of two men: a Benjamite (1 Chr 8:19) and a Levite (1 Chr 24:12)
gloss_readable: This personal name, meaning "he lifts up" or "he establishes," designates two individuals in the Chronicler's genealogies. The first appears in the Benjamite family tree, while the second represents a Levitical division in David's reorganization of temple service. The name has Sabaean parallels (Yahqam), showing its currency in the broader Semitic world. One occurrence includes a prepositional prefix ("for Yaqim"), indicating a lottery assignment for priestly courses.

senses.1: Attested in 1 Chronicles 8:19 and 24:12 for distinct individuals. The Septuagint renders it Iakeim (with variations), showing standard Greek transliteration practice. The two occurrences appear with different prefixes (conjunctive "and" and prepositional "for"), reflecting their different narrative contexts: genealogical listing versus priestly lot assignments.

gloss_terse: Aramaic adjective meaning honorable or difficult, depending on context
gloss_readable: This Aramaic loanword appears twice in biblical Aramaic sections, carrying two distinct but related meanings. In Ezra 4:10 it describes nobles or honorable persons who were deported, using the emphatic Aramaic form. In Daniel 2:11 it describes a difficult or hard matter, specifically the king's demand that his counselors reveal his dream without being told its content. The semantic range from "weighty" extends naturally to both social weight (honor) and practical weight (difficulty).

senses.1: Found in Ezra 4:10 (describing noble deportees) and Daniel 2:11 (describing a difficult request). The shift from honor to difficulty reflects the core sense of weightiness or significance. Spanish and English glosses distinguish the two uses (noble vs. difficult), while French and German preserve the Hebrew/Aramaic scripts, recognizing the Aramaic linguistic context of both passages.

gloss_terse: Yeqamam, a Levite mentioned in 1 Chronicles 23:19 and 24:23
gloss_readable: This personal name likely means "may the kinsman arise" or "let the people stand," according to BDB's analysis of its components. It designates a Levite from the Kohathite division, appearing in both the genealogical roster and the priestly course assignments. The Septuagint shows considerable variation (Ikemias, Iokom, Iakamias), reflecting the challenges of rendering Hebrew proper names in Greek.

senses.1: Attested in 1 Chronicles 23:19 and 24:23, both within Levitical genealogies. One occurrence includes the conjunctive prefix ("and Yeqamam"), showing the name's integration into list structures. Multilingual traditions maintain both forms, with French and German preserving Hebrew script in brackets to reflect the manuscript precision required for proper names.

gloss_terse: Yokmeam/Jokmeam, a city in northern Israel (1 Kgs 4:12) and a Levitical city of refuge in Ephraim (1 Chr 6:68)
gloss_readable: This place name may mean "let the people be established." It designates a city mentioned in Solomon's administrative districts, possibly the modern Tell Qaimun north of Megiddo. More significantly, it appears as a Levitical city of refuge in the tribal territory of Ephraim, where Chronicles identifies it as equivalent to Kibzaim from Joshua 21:22. The dual references suggest an important regional center with both administrative and religious functions.

senses.1: Found in 1 Kings 4:12 (administrative context) and 1 Chronicles 6:68 (Levitical cities). The Septuagint variations (Loukam, Oukam, Iekmaan) show the expected transliteration challenges. The identification with Kibzaim in Joshua links it to the cities of refuge network, giving it special status in ancient Israelite society as a place of asylum and Levitical residence.

gloss_terse: Yokte'el, two distinct locations: a town in Judah's Shephelah (Josh 15:38) and a renamed Petra (2 Kgs 14:7)
gloss_readable: This place name appears in two completely different contexts. First, as an unidentified town in the lowland region of Judah during the initial tribal allotments. Second, and more dramatically, as the new name given to Sela (Petra) by King Amaziah after capturing it from the Edomites. The renaming reflects ancient Near Eastern conquest practices where victors imposed new names to mark their dominion. The name's etymology remains uncertain, though it may be related to Yequthiel.

senses.1: Attested in Joshua 15:38 (Shephelah town) and 2 Kings 14:7 (renamed Petra). The two uses are geographically and historically distinct: one is a Judahite town of uncertain location, the other is the famous rock fortress in Edom. The Septuagint shows significant variation in both passages, reflecting the geographical distance between the two sites and the different historical contexts.

gloss_terse: Yiriyyah, a military officer during Jeremiah's time who arrested the prophet (Jer 37:13-14)
gloss_readable: This personal name, meaning "Yahweh sees," belongs to the captain of the guard who arrested the prophet Jeremiah when he attempted to leave Jerusalem during the Babylonian siege. Yiriyyah falsely accused Jeremiah of deserting to the Chaldeans, an accusation that led to the prophet's imprisonment. The name appears only in this brief but significant narrative, where a minor official plays a pivotal role in the suffering of God's spokesman.

senses.1: Found exclusively in Jeremiah 37:13-14 in the arrest narrative. The Septuagint renders it as Sarouias, showing significant departure from the Hebrew consonants. The officer's role is crucial to the Jeremiah narrative: his false accusation initiates a cycle of imprisonment and suffering that tests the prophet's resolve and demonstrates the hostility of Jerusalem's leadership to divine warning.

gloss_terse: Jareb, an epithet for an Assyrian king in Hosea 5:13 and 10:6; possibly means "contender" or "great king"
gloss_readable: This enigmatic term appears only in Hosea's oracles against Israel and Judah, where it designates an Assyrian monarch (likely Tiglath-Pileser III). The meaning is disputed: it may be a throne name meaning "one who contends," or it could be a corruption of the Assyrian title "great king" (šarru rabû). Modern scholars have proposed various emendations, including "Arabian king." The context emphasizes Israel's futile hope in foreign alliances rather than in Yahweh.

senses.1: Attested in Hosea 5:13 and 10:6 in parallel prophetic contexts. Both passages condemn reliance on Assyrian military power for healing and deliverance. The Hebrew tradition preserves it as a proper name, while French "contester" and German "streiten" translate it as a participle ("one who contends"), reflecting the interpretive uncertainty surrounding this hapax.

gloss_terse: Yerusha/Yerushah, mother of King Jotham, with variant spellings in 2 Kings 15:33 and 2 Chronicles 27:1
gloss_readable: This personal name, possibly meaning "possessed" or "married," designates the mother of Jotham, one of Judah's more faithful kings. The name appears with two spellings in the parallel accounts of Jotham's reign, a common phenomenon in the relationship between Kings and Chronicles. As a queen mother mentioned in the regnal formulae, she held significant status in Judahite court life, though no specific deeds are attributed to her.

senses.1: Found in 2 Kings 15:33 (Yerusha) and 2 Chronicles 27:1 (Yerushah), both in standard regnal introduction formulae. The variant spellings show the minor orthographic differences between the Deuteronomistic and Chronistic traditions. All multilingual glosses preserve both forms, recognizing the manuscript variation as historically authentic rather than an error requiring correction.

gloss_terse: Yerah, son of Joktan in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:26; 1 Chr 1:20)
gloss_readable: This personal name appears in the genealogy of Shem's descendants, specifically among the sons of Joktan who populated the Arabian peninsula. As an eponymous ancestor, Yerah likely represents a tribe or people group in ancient Arabia. The name's root connection to "moon" has led to speculation about lunar worship or a moon-related tribal identity, though the text itself offers no commentary on such associations.

senses.1: Attested in Genesis 10:26 and 1 Chronicles 1:20 within the Table of Nations. The Septuagint shows variation (Iarad vs. Iare/Iарех), with some manuscripts confusing this name with Jared. The context places Yerah among Joktan's thirteen sons, all of whom settled in the Arabian region "from Mesha toward Sephar," according to Genesis 10:30.

gloss_terse: Aramaic noun for "month"; appears in Ezra 6:15 and Daniel 4:29
gloss_readable: This Aramaic loanword for month appears in the biblical Aramaic sections of Ezra and Daniel. In Ezra it specifies the month of Adar when the temple was completed, while in Daniel it marks the passage of twelve months during Nebuchadnezzar's period of sanity before his humiliation. The word is the standard Aramaic equivalent to Hebrew "yerach" or "chodesh," showing the natural linguistic shift in the post-exilic period when Aramaic increasingly dominated Jewish linguistic life.

senses.1: Found in Ezra 6:15 (singular with preposition: "of the month") and Daniel 4:29 (plural: "months"). Both contexts involve calendrical precision: the completion date of the Second Temple and the duration of Nebuchadnezzar's interval before judgment. Multilingual traditions translate it straightforwardly as month/months, while French and German sometimes preserve the Aramaic form to signal the linguistic register.

gloss_terse: The Jerahmeelites, a clan or tribe in southern Judah mentioned in 1 Samuel 27:10 and 30:29
gloss_readable: This gentilics adjective designates a clan or tribal group dwelling in the Negev region of southern Judah during David's outlaw period. The Jerahmeelites appear among the groups David raided (or claimed to raid) while serving Achish of Gath, and later they received spoils from his Amalekite victory. Their connection to Jerahmeel son of Hezron (1 Chronicles 2) suggests they were a Judahite subgroup, though some scholars propose more complex tribal relationships in the pre-monarchic south.

senses.1: Attested in 1 Samuel 27:10 ("the Negeb of the Jerahmeelites") and 30:29 ("cities of the Jerahmeelites"). Both contexts place them in southern Judah's arid regions. The Septuagint shows confusion, rendering it variously as Iesmega, Israelites, Aermon, and Ieramehlei, suggesting Greek translators were uncertain about this southern tribal group's precise identity.

gloss_terse: Yarcha, an Egyptian slave who married into Sheshan's family (1 Chr 2:34-35)
gloss_readable: This personal name designates an Egyptian servant who received an unusual privilege: marriage to his master's daughter. Since Sheshan had no sons, he gave his daughter to Yarcha, thereby incorporating this foreigner into the Judahite lineage. The name appears with a prepositional prefix in one occurrence ("to Yarcha"), marking the marriage transaction. This narrative detail reveals the flexibility of genealogical boundaries and the importance of preserving family lines even through irregular means.

senses.1: Found in 1 Chronicles 2:34 and 35 within Sheshan's genealogy. The Septuagint variations (Iōchēl, Ieree) show transliteration uncertainty with this Egyptian name. The story is remarkable: a foreign slave becomes a legitimate ancestor in Judah's tribal records through marriage, demonstrating that genealogical incorporation could transcend ethnic boundaries when family continuity was at stake.

gloss_terse: Possession; used twice in Numbers 24:18 in Balaam's oracle about Edom and Seir becoming Israel's possession
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes possession or property, appearing in Balaam's climactic oracle where he prophesies Israel's future dominance over Edom and Seir. The word appears twice in the same verse in parallel constructions, emphasizing the totality of the conquest: both Edom and Seir will become Israel's possession. The prophecy found fulfillment in David's subjugation of Edom, making this oracle significant in understanding Israel's territorial expansion.

senses.1: Found exclusively in Numbers 24:18 in prophetic poetry. The double use creates poetic parallelism: "Edom shall be a possession, and Seir shall be a possession." The context is Balaam's final oracle, where despite being hired to curse Israel, he instead prophesies their triumph over surrounding nations. All major translations render it as possession, capturing the territorial conquest implied.

gloss_terse: Ishbi-benob, a Philistine giant who nearly killed David (2 Sam 21:16); textually problematic
gloss_readable: This name appears in the narrative of David's later battles with Philistine giants, where an aging David nearly falls to this warrior before Abishai rescues him. However, the text shows Ketiv/Qere variation, and many scholars believe it's corrupt. BDB proposes reading "and they dwelt in Gob," moving it to verse 15, which would eliminate the personal name entirely. The uncertainty reflects the textual difficulties in this section of 2 Samuel.

senses.1: Attested in 2 Samuel 21:16 with significant textual problems. The name literally means "dweller in Nob," but this makes little sense in context. Multilingual traditions show the confusion: Spanish offers both Yishbi and Yishvo forms in brackets, French preserves the Ketiv reading, and commentators widely suspect corruption. If genuine, it marks a significant moment when David's mortality became apparent to his men.

gloss_terse: Ishbak/Yishbaq, son of Abraham and Keturah (Gen 25:2; 1 Chr 1:32)
gloss_readable: This personal name designates one of Abraham's six sons by Keturah, his wife or concubine after Sarah's death. As an eponymous ancestor, Ishbak likely represents a northern Arabian tribe, though no clear identification has been established. The name appears in both the Genesis and Chronicles genealogies of Abraham's non-Israelite descendants, who received gifts and were sent eastward, away from Isaac.

senses.1: Found in Genesis 25:2 and 1 Chronicles 1:32 in parallel genealogies. One occurrence includes a conjunctive prefix ("and Yishbaq"), reflecting its position in the list of Keturah's sons. The Septuagint renders it Iesbōk (with variant Sobak in Chronicles), showing standard Greek transliteration. These sons of Keturah represent the genealogical explanation for various Arabian peoples known to ancient Israel.

gloss_terse: Yoshbeqashah, son of Heman the temple musician (1 Chr 25:4, 24)
gloss_readable: This personal name belongs to one of Heman's fourteen sons who served in temple music ministry during David's reign. The name appears both in the initial roster of Heman's sons and in the subsequent lot assignments determining their service order. The Septuagint shows considerable variation (Ieibaskatan, Bakata, Iesboka), reflecting the challenges of rendering this unusual compound name in Greek. Like his brothers, Yoshbeqashah represents the institutionalization of worship music in the Davidic temple preparations.

senses.1: Attested in 1 Chronicles 25:4 (genealogical list) and 25:24 (lot assignment). One occurrence has a prepositional prefix ("for Yoshbeqashah"), indicating the seventeenth lot in the musical service rotation. The name's length and form are unusual even among Heman's sons, many of whom bear compound or theophoric names that may encode prophetic or worshipful declarations.

gloss_terse: Ishvah/Yishvah, son of Asher in the tribal genealogies (Gen 46:17; 1 Chr 7:30)
gloss_readable: This personal name designates one of Asher's sons listed in both the descent to Egypt narrative and the Chronicles genealogies. Unlike his brothers Ishvi and Beriah, Ishvah receives no further mention or descendants in the biblical record, suggesting his line either died out early or was absorbed into other Asherite clans. The name appears with a conjunctive prefix in both occurrences, integrating it into the genealogical lists.

senses.1: Found in Genesis 46:17 and 1 Chronicles 7:30 in parallel genealogies of Asher. Both instances include the conjunction "and," placing Ishvah second in the list of Asher's sons. The Septuagint variations (Iessai, Isua, Iēsous) show the transliteration challenges, with some forms coincidentally resembling the name Jesus. The lack of descendants suggests Ishvah's line was not prominent in later Asherite history.

gloss_terse: Yishmayah/Yishmayahu, two men: a Gibeonite warrior (1 Chr 12:4) and a Zebulunite leader (1 Chr 27:19)
gloss_readable: This personal name, meaning "Yahweh hears," designates two individuals in the Chronicler's military and administrative records. The first was a Gibeonite warrior who joined David at Ziklag, numbered among the mighty men. The second served as tribal officer over Zebulun during David's kingdom organization. The name appears with slight orthographic variation (-yah vs. -yahu), showing the flexible theophoric endings common in biblical names.

senses.1: Attested in 1 Chronicles 12:4 (Gibeonite warrior) and 27:19 (Zebulunite officer). One occurrence includes a conjunctive prefix ("and Yishmayah"), while the other shows the longer theophoric form (-yahu). The Septuagint standardizes both as Samaias. These represent typical Chronicler inclusions: David's early supporters and later administrative organization, both emphasizing the king's comprehensive leadership structure.

gloss_terse: Jeshanah, a town on Ephraim's southern border (2 Chr 13:19) and possibly a gate in Jerusalem (Neh 12:39)
gloss_readable: This place name, meaning "old" or "ancient," designates a border town that Abijah captured from Jeroboam during the divided kingdom period. Located near Bethel, it's identified with modern Ain Siniya, about five miles north of Beitin. The name also appears in Nehemiah 12:39 as "the Old Gate" in Jerusalem's wall dedication, though the connection between the town and gate remains uncertain. Some scholars propose reading Jeshanah in place of "the Shen" in 1 Samuel 7:12.

senses.1: Found in 2 Chronicles 13:19 (town captured by Abijah) and Nehemiah 12:39 (possibly a gate name). The Nehemiah occurrence has the article ("the Old"), suggesting it may be descriptive rather than a proper name. The town marked Ephraim's southern boundary, making it strategically important in the northern kingdom's defenses against Judahite expansion.

gloss_terse: The Israelite, a gentilic adjective appearing in Leviticus 24:10 and possibly 2 Samuel 17:25
gloss_readable: This gentilic adjective designates someone as belonging to Israel, appearing in two notable contexts. In Leviticus 24:10-11 it describes both a man and a woman involved in the blasphemy incident that led to the death penalty legislation. The 2 Samuel occurrence is textually uncertain: the Masoretic text reads "the Ishmaelite" while the Septuagint and parallel in 1 Chronicles 2:19 support "the Israelite," creating interpretive challenges about Amasa's father's identity.

senses.1: Attested in Leviticus 24:10 (twice, masculine and feminine forms) and possibly 2 Samuel 17:25 (textual variant). The Leviticus context is crucial: it establishes that blasphemy law applies equally to Israelite and foreigner. The 2 Samuel reading affects whether Amasa's father was an Israelite or Ishmaelite, with significant implications for understanding David's family connections.

gloss_terse: Abundance, riches; appears in parallel oracles against Moab (Isa 15:7; Jer 48:36)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes abundance or accumulated wealth, appearing in nearly identical prophetic oracles against Moab. The phrase "the abundance they have acquired" describes the possessions Moabites will carry away in their flight from judgment. The parallel passages in Isaiah and Jeremiah show slight variation in vowel pointing (yithrah vs. yithrath), demonstrating the textual relationship between these two prophetic books while maintaining semantic equivalence.

senses.1: Found in Isaiah 15:7 and Jeremiah 48:36 in parallel Moab oracles. Both contexts describe fugitives carrying their accumulated wealth across the Brook of the Willows (or to the foundations). The construct form in Jeremiah shows the noun's grammatical flexibility. All major translations render it as abundance, surplus, or riches, capturing the sense of accumulated possessions now vulnerable to loss.

gloss_terse: Yithre'am/Yitream, David's sixth son born in Hebron (2 Sam 3:5; 1 Chr 3:3)
gloss_readable: This personal name designates the youngest of David's six sons born during his seven-year reign in Hebron, before he captured Jerusalem. His mother was Eglah, described as David's wife in a way that has sparked speculation about her possible identity with Michal. Yitream receives no further mention in biblical narrative, suggesting he died young or played no significant role in the succession struggles that dominate the later David story.

senses.1: Attested in 2 Samuel 3:5 and 1 Chronicles 3:3 in parallel birth lists. The Septuagint shows variation (Itharam, Iethraam), reflecting standard transliteration practice. As the sixth son, Yitream had no realistic claim to the throne, and his absence from later narratives stands in stark contrast to the prominence of Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah in the succession crisis.

gloss_terse: Yetheth/Jetheth, an Edomite chief listed in Genesis 36:40 and 1 Chronicles 1:51
gloss_readable: This personal name designates one of the Edomite chiefs descended from Esau, appearing in the genealogical lists that establish Edom's political structure before Israel had kings. The name appears in the formulaic roster of Edomite alluphs (chiefs or clan leaders), showing the parallel development of Edomite and Israelite societies. The Septuagint shows variation (Ieber, Iethet, Iether), reflecting the transliteration challenges with Edomite names.

senses.1: Found in Genesis 36:40 and 1 Chronicles 1:51 in parallel Edomite genealogies. Both contexts present him as one of the chiefs of Edom, part of the political organization that governed Esau's descendants. The lists emphasize that Edom developed structured leadership before Israel did ("before any king reigned over the Israelites"), an acknowledgment of Edomite political precedence.

gloss_terse: Glorious, honorable; feminine adjective describing a bed (Ezek 23:41) and a queen (Ps 45:13)
gloss_readable: This feminine adjective denotes something glorious or splendid, appearing in two poetic contexts. In Psalm 45:13 it describes the princess in her chamber, arrayed in glory for her wedding. In Ezekiel 23:41 it describes the bed on which unfaithful Jerusalem reclines in her idolatrous luxury. The word's vocalization (kevuddah) shows the construct form pattern, and its root connection to "glory" (kavod) links external splendor with inherent worth or honor.

senses.1: Attested in Psalm 45:13 (royal wedding psalm) and Ezekiel 23:41 (prophetic accusation). The contexts are ironically opposite: one celebrates legitimate royal splendor, the other condemns false glory in spiritual adultery. Spanish renders both as "gloriosa/glorioso," while French and German preserve Hebrew forms, acknowledging the specialized vocabulary of these poetic and prophetic passages.

gloss_terse: Cabul/Kavul, a border town in Asher (Josh 19:27) and a district Solomon gave to Hiram (1 Kgs 9:13)
gloss_readable: This place name designates both a specific town and a broader district in Galilee. The town served as a boundary marker for Asher's tribal territory, identified with modern Kabul about nine miles southeast of Acre. More famously, it names the twenty-city district Solomon gave King Hiram as payment for temple construction materials, which Hiram rejected as inadequate. The folk etymology suggests "as good as nothing" (ke + bal), explaining Hiram's displeasure, though this may be popular wordplay rather than true etymology.

senses.1: Found in Joshua 19:27 (Asher's border) and 1 Kings 9:13 (district given to Hiram). The Kings passage preserves the negative assessment: Hiram saw the cities and they did not please him, calling them "the land of Cabul." The etymological wordplay suggests the name became synonymous with worthlessness, at least in this transaction, though the actual town remained a legitimate settlement in Asher.

gloss_terse: A woven covering, either a quilt or mosquito net made of goats' hair (1 Sam 19:13, 16)
gloss_readable: This masculine noun designates a woven goat-hair covering that Michal used to simulate David's presence in bed when deceiving Saul's messengers. Scholars debate whether it was a thick quilt or a mosquito net spread over the face during sleep. The phrase "quilt of goats" or "goats' hair net" appears identically in both verses. Either interpretation explains how Michal created the illusion of David lying ill in bed while he escaped.

senses.1: Attested in 1 Samuel 19:13 and 16 in the David escape narrative. One occurrence includes a conjunctive prefix ("and a pillow of"). The root suggests something netted or woven, making both quilt and fly-net plausible. All major translations preserve the ambiguity with terms like "pillow," "quilt," or "woven covering," acknowledging that ancient bedding vocabulary doesn't map neatly onto modern categories.

gloss_terse: Fetters, shackles; used in parallel with iron chains in Psalms 105:18 and 149:8
gloss_readable: This masculine noun denotes fetters or shackles, appearing in two psalms with quite different contexts. In Psalm 105:18 it describes Joseph's imprisonment in Egypt, where his feet were bound with fetters and iron. In Psalm 149:8 it appears in the triumphant vision of Israel binding enemy kings with fetters of iron. The word is late biblical Hebrew, appearing only in these poetic contexts where it parallels "iron" and "chains."

senses.1: Found in Psalm 105:18 (Joseph's affliction) and Psalm 149:8 (eschatological judgment). Both passages use "fetters" in parallel with iron, emphasizing the material and security of the binding. The singular collective in Psalm 105 ("they humbled his feet with fetters") contrasts with the construct plural in Psalm 149 ("with fetters of iron"), showing the noun's grammatical flexibility in poetic parallelism.

gloss_terse: A precious stone, possibly ruby or carnelian; mentioned in Isaiah 54:12 and Ezekiel 27:16
gloss_readable: This masculine noun designates a precious stone, most likely ruby or carnelian, valued for its red sparkle. In Isaiah 54:12 it appears in God's promise to rebuild Zion with precious stones, making her battlements of rubies. In Ezekiel 27:16 it's listed among the luxury goods traded with Tyre. The word has Aramaic cognates (kadkadana), suggesting it was a technical trade term for a specific gemstone in the ancient Near Eastern luxury commerce.

senses.1: Attested in Isaiah 54:12 (Zion's restoration) and Ezekiel 27:16 (Tyre's trade). Both contexts emphasize precious value and beauty. Spanish renders it as "ruby" in both passages, French as "grenade" (garnet), and German preserves the Hebrew form, reflecting the uncertainty about which specific red gemstone the ancient term designated. The Isaiah context particularly emphasizes transformation: God will make Zion's very fortifications out of gems.

gloss_terse: To burn, scorch, brand; Niphal stem meaning to be scorched or burned (Prov 6:28; Isa 43:2)
gloss_readable: This verb denotes burning or scorching, appearing only in the Niphal (passive/reflexive) stem in biblical Hebrew. In Proverbs 6:28 it appears in a rhetorical question about walking on hot coals: will a man's feet not be burned? In Isaiah 43:2 God promises Israel protection in trial: when you walk through fire, you shall not be scorched. Both contexts use fire metaphorically, Proverbs for sexual sin's consequences and Isaiah for divine preservation through persecution.

senses.1: Found in Proverbs 6:28 (wisdom warning) and Isaiah 43:2 (salvation oracle). The Proverbs passage uses second person ("shall... be burned") in hypothetical questioning, while Isaiah uses masculine plural ("they shall not be scorched") in parallel with the verb "to burn" (ba'ar). All major translations render it as scorch, burn, or singe, capturing the fire damage to living tissue.

gloss_terse: A burn, burning; noun used in the lex talionis formula "burn for burn" (Exod 21:25)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun designates a burn injury, appearing only in Exodus 21:25 within the famous lex talionis (law of retaliation) formula. The phrase "burn for burn" completes the sequence "eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe." The principle established proportional justice, limiting revenge to equivalence rather than escalation. The word derives from the same root as the verb "to burn" discussed above.

senses.1: Attested exclusively in Exodus 21:25, appearing twice in the construct phrase "burn for burn." All major translations preserve the repetitive formula ("quemadura por quemadura" in Spanish, "brûler pour brûler" in French, "verbrennen für verbrennen" in German), recognizing the legal precision of the lex talionis principle that requires exact correspondence between injury and recompense.
